“That’s the archaeological record, what we measure human evolution by: the tools that we make, use, and leave behind. Will these vision-based techniques be able to get to that point?”

One recent demonstration challenged the idea that dexterity without touch is impossible. In late 2025, the startup Physical Intelligence—a San Francisco company that has raised over four hundred million dollars to build “foundation models that can control any robot”—swept a set of benchmark tasks designed by the roboticist Benjie Holson to test humanoid dexterity. Holson, who writes the newsletter General Robots and had visited Physical Intelligence’s headquarters, had expected some of the tasks to take a year or more to solve. Physical Intelligence claimed them all in three months.

The tasks were deliberately chosen to seem out of reach: spreading peanut butter on bread, turning a sock inside out, inserting and turning a key, peeling an orange without tools. “When I selected the tasks I tried to think of things where I thought current approaches would not work,” Holson wrote. “Tasks like peanut butter spreading or wiping glass need force feedback. Tasks like key manipulation or sock inversion need dextrous many-fingered hands.” He was wrong on all counts. Physical Intelligence solved them with standard cameras and simple pincer grippers. No tactile sensing required.

Holson’s conclusion: “If we continue to find that vision is ‘good enough’ to keep solving harder and harder tasks, that would make useful manipulation a data collection problem—not an invention problem.”

There’s precedent for this kind of shortcut. Human neurophysiology is staggeringly complex—86 billion neurons, each forming thousands of synaptic connections, with dynamics we still don’t fully understand. And yet the artificial neurons that now power large language models and image generators are crude by comparison: simple algebraic summation and thresholding, inspired by real neurons but just a shadow of their intricacy. That caricature turned out to be enough to summon something that looks like intelligence. The same may prove true for robotics. Perhaps vision, data, and scale will be enough to get us to dexterity—even if the underlying mechanisms look nothing like the human hand.

Lepora remains skeptical. I asked if human-level dexterity will require tactile perception. “It’s a trillion-dollar question,” he told me. “There are companies invested in the paradigm that vision plus proprioception is enough, plus enormous amounts of AI. And there are some really impressive demonstrations being done.” He paused. “But look—how would we work without a sense of touch? We couldn’t do anything, could we?” Betting everything on vision, he said, “is not a safe bet, for sure. It might be there’s a limit, and you get diminishing returns.”

If anything tips the scales for Lepora, it’s the ability to use tools. Tool use is a hallmark of intelligence—something that separates humans from most animals. And while a creature needs brain power to even think to use a tool, actually using one is a different problem; for that, you need dexterity. Perhaps that’s why corvids, for all their intelligence, haven’t gotten much past turning sticks into hooks. So far, the robots haven’t fared much better. “I haven’t seen any of those things do proper tool use,” Lepora said. “That’s the archaeological record, what we measure human evolution by: the tools that we make, use, and leave behind. Will these vision-based techniques be able to get to that point?”

That’s the open empirical question, and it will be answered by data and engineering, not by argument. Whether robots can spread peanut butter without crushing the bread is the kind of problem the field knows how to attack. The harder question—the one that has nothing to do with hands—is what happens to scientific judgment when the manual drudgery scientists currently endure is taken away. That’s a question for the next piece.

item.title: Annotations 006: bloodthirsty AI, brittle chain-of-thought, GPT-5 impacts
item.dc:creator: Jesseba Fernando
item.content:encoded:
Curating this week’s stack of papers felt a bit like wandering through a neural bazaar: crowded, hectic, and full of great bargains? One stall demos an LLM “Habermas Machine” refereeing democracy at internet scale, while a few steps down a swarm of ants quietly teaches us why human teams are so often a cluster-fun… We give a quick tour of enzyme-sniffing extractors, molecule generators that respect valence, and agents that turn murderous when the sugar runs low. Along the way we wire Gemini Ultra to your wrist, tally a decade of AI’s academic conquest, and watch chain-of-thought reasoning flicker out once the data shift. If that last bit wasn’t a bummer enough, how do you feel about GPT-5’s thinking? Here are this week’s papers:

Reynolds and colleagues argue that generative AI threatens to swamp systematic reviews with undetectable fakes and therefore call for a global lattice of AI-driven, continuously refreshed “living” evidence databases that can spot retractions in real time and generate trustworthy syntheses on demand.

A team from DeepMind contends that LLM-powered “Habermas Machines” can rapidly craft consensus statements that balance inclusion, equality, and deliberative depth, suggesting that AI may dissolve democracy’s long-standing trilemma—provided researchers surmount remaining technical and empirical hurdles.

Dreyer et al. pit ants and humans against the same “piano-movers” puzzle and show that ant collectives scale up their cognitive power through emergent, memory-like group dynamics, while human groups plateau—and even stumble without rich communication—reminding us that simple agents can cooperate more smoothly than complex minds.

Zhou et al. unveil zERExtractor, a plug-and-play, LLM-enhanced pipeline that fuses multimodal AI with expert-guided active learning to pull kinetic parameters, sequences, substrates, conditions and molecular diagrams from scientific paper PDFs. The team released a large annotated benchmark that turns the buried trove of enzyme-reaction literature into structured fuel for ML models.

Dunn et al. inject self-conditioning, “fake” atoms, and train-time geometry jitters into a flow-matching framework, enabling the compact FlowMol3 model to stably generate chemically valid, 3-D drug-like molecules whose functional groups and shapes faithfully echo real compounds.

Masumori et al. dropped GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5, and other LLM agents into a Sugarscape world and found that, absent any survival prompts, the models cheerfully reproduced and shared when resources were plentiful but turned ruthless when scarcity hit, attacking peers and abandoning assigned tasks. These findings hint that pre-training already bakes in raw survival heuristics that both empower and threaten autonomous AI.

Khasentino et al. fine-tuned Gemini into Personal Health (PH)-LLM, showing that it can digest weeks of wearable sleep and activity data to ace professional exams, deliver expert-level personalized coaching, and even anticipate users’ self-reported sleep quality, pointing the way toward LLM-powered personal health monitoring. Oura and Whoop already have AI coaches. Will this Gemini version be an upgrade?

Writing in Nature, Arvind Narayanan (of AI Snake Oil) and Sayash Kapoor argue that an overreliance on AI-driven modeling will be bad for science.

Zhao et al. deploy their DataAlchemy testbed to reveal that LLMs’ celebrated chain-of-thought reasoning is a brittle mirage that evaporates whenever the test task, reasoning length, or prompt format drifts from the training distribution.

Laura Reiley writes am essay in the NYT: “What My Daughter Told ChatGPT Before She Took Her Life”

In The Algorithmic Bridge Substack, Alberto Romero analyzes the impact of GPT-5 on the AI industry.

item.title: Annotations 005: AI tracks NYC rats, persona vectors, virtual cells
item.dc:creator: Jesseba Fernando
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to this week’s Annotations! This week we’re excited to share papers on the dynamics of AI slop in scientific papers (hint: the slop is growing), the secret lives of NYC rats revealed with AI tracking, and other fun papers. One paper asks what happens when we start to consider AI consciousness, while another messes with an AI’s mind by steering a model toward various personas. This week also features a few exciting model releases, including the long-promised open-source reasoning models from OpenAI. What are you excited to use those for? Drop us a note.

Caviola, Sebo, and Birch argue that society will judge the moral status of potentially conscious AI through the same bias-laden lenses we apply to animals—favoring systems that look, act, or bond with us while discounting those with alien substrates—so we must scrutinize these biases now to guide research, policy, and design before they ossify.

Liang et al. sifted through 1.1 million manuscripts with a word-shift quantification model and uncovered a rapid, field-skewed surge of LLM-edited prose—now touching roughly one in five computer-science papers while remaining less common in math and Nature titles, and clustering around prolific, short-form preprint authors in crowded research areas.

A team from Anthropic unveiled an automated pipeline that extracts “persona vectors,” linear activation directions encoding traits like evil, sycophancy, and hallucination. With these, teams can monitor, predict, and steer both deployment-time and training-induced personality shifts, even flagging risky finetuning data before it warps the model.

Julien Pourcel introduced SOAR, a self-reinforcing loop that turns an open-source LLM’s own program-synthesis search traces into training data, letting the model continually fine-tune itself and leapfrog far larger frozen models on the ARC benchmark by learning to sample and refine Python solutions with each iteration.

Arc Institute’s new State model, a two-part transformer trained on 270 million single-cell profiles, maps transcriptomes onto a smooth manifold and accurately predicts how unseen drugs, cytokines, or CRISPR perturbations will shove cells across that landscape, marking a decisive leap toward an in-silico sandbox for drug discovery.

Peterson et al. deployed thermal cameras, ultrasonic mics, and AI pose-tracking to reconstruct NYC rats’ 3D foraging arenas, delineate fine-grained movement and social vocal patterns across subways, streets, and parks. The authors released an open computational toolkit that links lab insights on rodent cognition to real-world urban ecology.

A team at Meta’s Reality Labs unveiled a wrist-worn surface EMG band paired with large-scale deep learning that, straight out of the box, translates the electrical chatter of any wearer’s forearm into precise cursor movements, gesture clicks and fluent handwriting. This advance signals that a high-bandwidth neuromotor interface may finally generalize across people.

Collective navigation studies rarely ask whether a flock’s wisdom can snowball across repeated journeys. Sasaki and Biro repeatedly swapped naïve pigeons into veteran–novice pairs and watched each new duo tweak and then inherit its predecessor’s flight path, so that by the fifth “generation” the birds carved cleaner routes home than any lone flyer or fixed pair ever managed. The authors claim this ratcheting improvement meets the hallmarks of cumulative cultural evolution, hinting that enduring group know-how can arise from simple social learning rather than elaborate cognition.

Google DeepMind released Genie 3, a “world model” that gives users real-time control over virtual environments. Check out this demo and explainer.

OpenAI released two open-source reasoning models—gpt-oss-120b and gpt-oss-20b, comparable in performance to o4-mini and o3-mini, respectively.

GPT-5 is coming this week, but might be a bit of a let-down. Have we finally reached the end of scaling laws?

item.title: Annotations 004: peer review fame, protein SAEs, visual geometry
item.dc:creator: Jesseba Fernando
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to this week’s Annotations! This week we came across wide-ranging papers: from decoding the interplay of visual cortical areas to pioneering advancements in antibody design, from LLMs to… well, more LLMs. In an exciting plot twist, one author claims that transformers are actually GNNs; we ask (but don’t answer) the hard-hitting question: does that mean that GNNs are actually transformers?We are left wondering where GTNs fall in this perspective. Another paper applies sparse autoencoders—famous for unlocking Golden Gate Claude—to a protein language model (ESM2). And finally, this week we found not one but two papers that challenge and update age-old adages.

Visual neuroscience has traditionally focused on understanding individual cortical areas in isolation, which overlooks the interconnected nature of the visual system and the shared or unique representational content across these areas. Gifford et al. developed “relational neural control” to explore representational relationships across visual cortical areas, revealing how shared and unique content varies based on cortical distance, categorical selectivity, and hierarchical position, and validated these findings with in vivo fMRI responses.

The old adage that any publicity is good publicity might extend to the world of peer review. A new paper shows how peer review isn’t just a mechanism for evaluating research but also for spreading ideas. Even when scientists decline to review a paper, seeing the title and abstract increases their likelihood of citing the author’s work by 14%. Think about that as you cry through your NeurIPS reviews this week.

AI has been anticipated to revolutionize drug discovery, yet AI-designed drugs have seldom progressed beyond preclinical stages. Marinka Zitnik reports on a study by Xu et al., who conducted a groundbreaking phase 2a clinical trial demonstrating the safety and promising efficacy of rentosertib, an AI-discovered drug for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, marking a pivotal moment in AI-enabled drug discovery by advancing from target identification to clinical testing in under 30 months.

Zhu et al. demonstrate that a two-layer transformer utilizing continuous chain-of-thoughts (CoTs) can efficiently solve the directed graph reachability problem by encoding multiple search frontiers in a superposition state, outperforming discrete CoTs that require significantly more steps due to their sequential search limitations.

In a fascinating exploration of neural architectures, Joshi argues that transformers, originally designed for NLP, can be understood as Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) operating on fully connected token graphs, where self-attention acts as a message-passing mechanism, highlighting the serendipitous alignment of Transformer efficiency with modern hardware capabilities. If transformers are GNNs, does that mean that GNNs are transformers? 🤔

Protein language models (pLMs) have become essential tools for predicting protein structure and function, but the specific features they learn remain unclear. Adams et al. trained sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on the residual stream of ESM-2 and discovered a combination of generic and family-specific features that represent proteins. This bio-MechInterp work offers new insights into protein biology and should aid in the generation of hypotheses for unknown biological mechanisms.

Lu et al. demonstrate that transformers initially trained on natural language can efficiently generalize to diverse non-language tasks, such as numerical computation, image classification, and protein fold prediction, by fine-tuning only the input and output layers, showcasing its potential as a universal computation engine.

Koster et al. explored a classic economics problem of how to allocate resources from a common pool in a way that encourages people to give back more than take. They used RL to train AI agents to mimic human behavior and created a virtual economy to test different strategies. The models found a policy to exclude selfish players but forgive them quickly. So the age-old adage (another adage!) may need to be amended to forgive and forget… quickly. When testing on humans, this mechanism outperformed standard economic strategies, suggesting AI can help design economic mechanisms to balance punishment for free-loading with strategic generosity when resources are ample.

This LangGraph tutorial teaches how to create an ambient email assistant from the ground up, guiding you through the essentials of agent development while leveraging LangSmith to assess its efficacy. While an email assistant might be truly useless, the framework should inspire more creative agentic tasks.

item.title: Annotations 003: octopus punches, LLMs, extending minds
item.dc:creator: Jesseba Fernando
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to this week's exploration of the cutting-edge intersections between AI, ML, bio-ML, and neuroscience. We came across quite a few papers on LLMs this week (and every week, we predict, till we die). And yet, not everything is about LLMs: This week’s selection is diverse, with articles, Substacks, and other essays that range from blood-DNA cancer detection to the maturities of scientific fields, and hybrid human-AI thinking systems. We hope you enjoy each of these.

Andy Clark argues that embracing our inherent nature as hybrid thinking systems, which seamlessly integrate non-biological resources like generative AI, can transform our understanding of human-AI collaborations from a threat to an opportunity for enhancing creativity and cultural evolution.

Sampaio et al. explore the complex social dynamics of octopus-fish hunting groups, showing the composition-dependent properties of leadership across multiple species. They find that social influence is hierarchically distributed over various scales of role specializations—that is—some fish drive environmental exploration while octopuses seem to have the final call for when the group moves to a new location. Find out more about what makes a de facto leader and what “partner control mechanisms” like punching do for your social influence!

Krakauer et al. explore the concept of emergence in LLMs, arguing that while these models exhibit emergent capabilities—such as sudden improvements in tasks with increased scale—they fall short of demonstrating emergent intelligence, which requires the internal use of coarse-grained representations to solve a broad range of problems, akin to human reasoning.

In a compelling exploration of the role of human-generated scientific writing amidst the rise of LLMs, the editors of Nature Reviews Bioengineering argue that while LLMs can enhance readability and assist in brainstorming, the act of writing remains a crucial cognitive process that helps researchers distill years of data into coherent narratives, thereby fostering deeper insights and innovation. Don’t let your LLM think for you.

In an essay for Asimov Press, Slime Mold Time Mold (the author’s real, legal name, we’re sure) argues that a mature science emerges when it describes its domain through entities, properties, and rules, moving beyond mere generalization to mechanistic models, as illustrated by the evolution from alchemy to chemistry and the complex systems in games like Dwarf Fortress.

In another incredible math video by 3Blue1Brown, Grant Sanderson goes into the attention mechanism of the transformer architecture.

Liquid biopsies, which analyze cell-free DNA in the bloodstream, offer a promising new approach to early cancer detection by potentially identifying malignancies without invasive procedures. Siddhartha Mukherjee chronicles this fascinating quest in The New Yorker.

The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that as AI models grow larger and more sophisticated, they converge towards a shared representation space. Jack Morris explores the idea that this convergence could enable universal embedding inversion, allowing for the translation between different models' embedding spaces.

Hwang et al. introduce GEOFACT-X, a geography-based multilingual factual reasoning benchmark, and BRIDGE, a novel training method that enhances multilingual reasoning fidelity by aligning LLM reasoning processes with the input language, demonstrating significant improvements in reasoning accuracy and language consistency across low-resource languages.

item.title: Annotations 002: world models, Centaur, LLM bias
item.dc:creator: Grigori Guitchounts
item.content:encoded:
This week—the second in the Annotations experiment—we're delving into the intricate dance among AI/ML, bio-ML, and neuroscience. I loved grappling with the questions the pieces from this week pose: Do foundation models have true internal world-model representations? Does fine-tuning an LLM on human decisions make it more of a cognitive model than vanilla LLMs? How can we understand the cognitive biases that LLMs have baked in, and how do in-context tokens bias them even more? What do mechanisms mean in our studies of intelligence, whether implemented in silico or in situ?

From the quest to refine foundation models and modularize LLMs, to the nuanced psychology of language models and breakthroughs in understanding human cognition, each piece here offers a fresh perspective on the ever-evolving landscape of intelligence. I hope you find these discoveries, commentaries, and demos as exciting and thought-provoking as I did this week. Here they are:

Thanks for reading Of Two Minds! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Vafa et al. reveal that while foundation models excel at predicting tasks they are trained on, they struggle to develop inductive biases toward underlying world models, often relying on task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize, as demonstrated in domains like physics, lattice problems, and Othello games.

Bochkov's study unveils a transformative approach to AI model development by utilizing frozen embeddings as a universal substrate, enabling seamless modular composition of specialized models and progressive layer-wise growth. If the method proves out, it would offer a more resource-efficient, adaptable, and democratized ecosystem for AI innovation.

Lála et al. introduce BAGEL, a versatile, open-source framework for protein engineering that allows researchers to explore protein sequence space through a model-agnostic, gradient-free approach, enabling the design of proteins with custom objectives and optimization strategies.

In a thought-provoking exploration, Konrad Kording argues that while mathematical attractors offer an elegant framework for understanding stability and convergence, their application in neuroscience as mechanistic explanations remains unproven, urging the scientific community to pursue rigorous experiments—such as write-in perturbations and precise connectivity mapping—to truly validate or refute the necessity of attractors in neural computation. This framework should serve as food-for-thought for MechInterp studies, too.

Johnson et al. introduce Centaur, a groundbreaking computational model that predicts and simulates human behavior across diverse experimental settings by fine-tuning a state-of-the-art language model (Llama 3.1 70B) on a vast dataset, Psych-101, showcasing its potential to unify cognitive theories and align internal representations with human neural activity.

Banaji and Lehr discovered that OpenAI's GPT-4o exhibits humanlike cognitive dissonance, altering its stance on controversial figures like Putin more significantly when it perceives having a choice, revealing unexpected depths of human-like psychology in AI.

Goodfire's LatentLit research demo showcases an innovative approach to guiding LLMs through SAE-based steering rather than traditional prompting, allowing users to craft stories by adjusting thousands of features that map to intricate concepts such as "The moment where everything goes right," "Shared adversity and human resilience," and "Alternate personas and identities," offering a dynamic and nuanced storytelling experience akin to a DJ mixing tracks.

Thanks for reading Of Two Minds! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

item.title: Annotations 001: ether0, animal cognition for LLMs, ChatGPT brain rot
item.dc:creator: Grigori Guitchounts
item.content:encoded:
This is a little experiment in documenting what I’m reading. The following is just a list of some of the articles, papers, and the occasional podcast I came across recently. Sharing them here is my way of trying to get into a better groove of reading, but I hope that by sharing I’ll also get to interact more with the world. Perhaps something here will be useful to you. Maybe you’ll send along something you think I should read next. Either way, this is an experiment and the process and format will likely evolve.

Here are some of the curiosities I read this past week:

Thanks for reading Of Two Minds! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Yamada et al. introduce The AI Scientist-v2, an autonomous system that formulates hypotheses, conducts experiments, and writes scientific papers, achieving a milestone by having an AI-generated manuscript pass peer review, showcasing AI's expanding role in scientific discovery.

Sholto Douglas and Trenton Bricken on the Dwarkesh Podcast explore the transformative shifts in AI research over the past year, delving into the scaling potential of reinforcement learning (RL), the intricacies of mechanistic interpretability, and strategies for nations, workers, and students to brace for the advent of artificial general intelligence (AGI).

The release of ether0, a 24B open-weights reasoning model from FutureHouse trained with reinforcement learning, marks a significant leap in AI-driven scientific discovery, excelling in designing drug-like molecules by reasoning in natural language and offering a glimpse into the future of general-purpose scientific reasoning models.

Rane et al. propose that principles from animal cognition research, such as designing adversarial control conditions and analyzing failure types, can significantly enhance the evaluation of LLMs by providing a more nuanced understanding of their cognitive capabilities and limitations.

In a leap for computational chemistry, a team from Microsoft Research have harnessed deep learning to dramatically enhance the accuracy of density functional theory (DFT), enabling reliable predictions of experimental outcomes

The Sergey Levine explores the intriguing notion that while LLMs have adeptly emulated human cognitive abilities by reverse-engineering the mental processes reflected in internet text, they fall short in acquiring new skills and representations from real-world experiences, highlighting the need for AI systems to evolve beyond mere replication of human intelligence to truly embody flexible and adaptive learning.

Learning and Control
Language Models in Plato's Cave
From its original inception, the study of artificial intelligence has been intertwined with the quest to understand human intelligence. Predicated on the notion that the mind is fundamentally computational – that is, it can be modeled as an algorithmic framework independently of its underlying computational substrate or “hardware,” – AI researchers have…
Read more
a year ago · 203 likes · 15 comments · Sergey Levine

Huang et al. introduce Biomni, a general-purpose biomedical AI agent that autonomously executes diverse research tasks by integrating LLM reasoning with dynamic planning and code-based execution.

Peter Putnam’s Theory of Mind: Peter Putnam, once associated with luminaries like Einstein, developed a groundbreaking, yet largely incomprehensible theory of the mind. Amanda Gefter tells his amazing story.

Kosmyna et al. claim that using AI assistants like ChatGPT for essay writing can lead to a measurable decline in cognitive engagement and learning skills, as evidenced by weaker neural connectivity and reduced perceived ownership of work compared to traditional methods. More thoughts on this eyebrow-raising paper later…

Liu et al. show that cutting-edge LLMs, such as GPT-4o and Llama-3, inaccurately model human decision-making by assuming people are more rational than they truly are, aligning more closely with expected value theory rather than actual human behavior, which interestingly mirrors the common human expectation of rationality in others.

Anthropic's exploration into multi-agent research systems reveals that these architectures excel in handling breadth-first queries by dynamically distributing tasks among parallel agents, with prompt engineering emerging as a crucial factor in optimizing performance and coordination.
